title: Partner channel quarterly review: Q3
scratchpad:
Q3: 19 partner deals (not 23 - 4 double counted w/ direct), 168k
Tillerman 11/19
referral fee 12% (not 15), paid after 1st invoice, from Jan 1
Northgable 20% margin, min 5 deals/yr (asked 30)
tracks: Referral + Reseller (no bronze/silver/gold)
co-marketing Q4 = 10k (Ilse asked 18k), 6k Tillerman open days
Dagny: Northgable contract Thu 22nd
segments: Okay, let's start. This is the partner review for Q3. Dagny, it's your meeting really, I'm just here to make sure we leave with decisions.
Thanks. The plan is results first, then the three things partners keep asking about: the referral fee, Northgable's reseller terms, and co-marketing money for Q4.
And the program structure. You sent a proposal with tiers in it, and I have opinions about that.
I'd be worried if you didn't. We'll get to it. Ilse's here for the marketing part, and Elena because half of these deals touch her team.
Hi all. I've got the co-marketing requests in a spreadsheet, so shout when we get there.
Quick reminder of who we're talking about. Three active partners. Tillerman Supply, the parts distributor, which refers its contractor customers to us.
Northgable Systems, the integrator, who set up software for mid-sized fleets and want to resell us. And the Lantern Trades Guild, the heating engineers' association.
There's also a fourth partner on paper. A van-fitting company signed a referral agreement in July and hasn't sent a single introduction since.
Then they're not a partner, they're a signature. Do we chase them, or let it lapse quietly?
I'll have one more call with them this month. If nothing comes of it, we let the agreement lapse at the end of the year and stop counting them.
Fair. One call, then let it lapse. I'd rather report three real partners than four on paper.
Okay, that's the cast. Results, please, and the headline number first.
Q3 was our best quarter yet. Twenty three partner-sourced deals, worth two hundred and ten thousand dollars in new annual contract value.
That's a big jump from last quarter, if I remember the numbers right. What was it in Q2?
Fourteen deals. So the number of deals is up by more than half, and most of the growth came in August and September.
Is some of that seasonal? Contractors get busier in the autumn, so they may be more open to software then.
Some of it. Q3 is always busier than Q2 for the trades. But Tillerman's branch staff only started mentioning us in July, so most of it is real.
Can I flag something before that number goes anywhere? I went through the list last night, and some of those deals look familiar.
At least a few of them were also logged by my team as direct deals. Same customer, same contract, credited twice.
That's possible. The partner tracking and the sales pipeline are two different reports, and nobody reconciles them.
How many are we talking about? One or two is noise. Ten would change the whole story.
Let me check properly before I say a number. Give me a few minutes, I've got both reports open side by side.
While Elena checks, Dagny, which partner did the most?
Tillerman, by a distance. Their branch staff mention us every time a contractor asks about scheduling, and it's starting to show in the numbers.
Northgable is slower. Their deals are bigger, but they're long, and a couple of them are still in contracting with the customer's procurement team.
And the Guild deals are small shops, mostly one or two engineers. Lots of interest, small contracts.
Which is fine, as long as small shops don't cost us more to support than they pay.
On that, I pulled support numbers for partner customers too. The Tillerman referrals open about as many tickets as our direct customers in their first month.
The Guild shops open more, mostly basic questions. One-person businesses don't have an office manager to read the help articles for them.
That's exactly what proper onboarding would fix. A small shop that's been shown the basics doesn't email support about them.
Keep that thought for when we get to the Guild. It's relevant there.

Okay, I've got it. Four of Dagny's twenty three were also logged as direct deals. Take those out and partners brought in nineteen deals in Q3, worth a hundred and sixty eight thousand dollars in new annual contract value.
Nineteen. Okay, that's less exciting, but it's still well up on Q2. I'd rather report the real number than have someone in finance find the double counting for us in January.
Agreed. Report nineteen, and the hundred and sixty eight thousand. And let's fix the counting so we're not doing this again next quarter.
With the corrected list, Tillerman Supply brought in eleven of the nineteen deals. All four of the double counted ones were Northgable or Guild deals, not Tillerman.
So Tillerman is more than half the channel on its own. That's worth knowing before we change anything about the fee.
On the counting, the fix is deal registration. A partner registers a deal before the first demo, and if they don't, the deal is direct.
Partners will push back on before the first demo. Sometimes they make the introduction and only remember to tell us a week later.
Then within a week of the first demo. But there has to be a cutoff, or we'll be arguing about credit forever.
Okay. Partners register a deal within a week of the first demo. If it isn't registered by then, it counts as direct. Elena, can you build the form?
Yes. I'll set up a registration form in the CRM, linked to the pipeline, by Friday the thirtieth of October.
Good, that solves the counting for next quarter. Referral fee. Dagny, what are partners asking for?
Today we pay ten percent of the first-year contract value, at signature. Tillerman told me last month that other software vendors they work with pay more.
My proposal is to raise it to fifteen percent for all partners. It's simple, it's competitive, and it keeps Tillerman's branch staff motivated.
I'm going to push back on fifteen percent. Partner deals already cost us more to close than direct ones. We still do the demo, the security questions and the whole onboarding.
A referral is an introduction, not a sale. Fifteen percent for an introduction is more than we spend on marketing per deal on our own.
But without the introduction there's no deal at all. Most of Tillerman's contractors would never have found us otherwise.
Can I suggest something on timing rather than the percentage? Today we pay at signature. We've paid out on two deals that never paid their first invoice.
That's money we'll never see again. I'd much rather pay referral fees on customers who actually pay us.
So pay the fee once the customer has paid their first invoice. That protects us, and partners don't lose anything on good deals.
Partners will accept that if the percentage moves. If I go back with no change in the number and a later payment, they'll feel worse off.
For what it's worth, Tillerman cares more about the number being easy to explain to their branch staff than about it being high.
Then something in between. Not fifteen. Something that's a clear improvement on ten without giving the margin away.
Twelve? It's a real increase, it's easy to say, and with the payment moving to after the first invoice, the cost to us is about the same as ten today.
I can live with twelve if it's paid after the first invoice. Not at signature. And I'd want that written into every partner agreement, not just the new ones.
Okay. The referral fee becomes twelve percent of first-year contract value, paid once the customer has paid its first invoice. It applies to deals registered from the first of January.
Good. I'll tell Tillerman this week, before they hear it from anyone else.
How do we actually pay these? Today it's Greta's team doing a manual transfer whenever someone remembers to ask.
Once a month, on one statement per partner. Every deal that paid its first invoice that month, the fee for each, and the total.
The statement can come straight out of the registration form and the billing system, as long as the form records the partner on the deal.
Good. One monthly statement per partner, generated, not typed. Dagny, check the format with Greta before the first one goes out.
Will do. The first statement under the new terms would go out in February, for January's deals.
Next, program structure. Dagny, walk us through the tiers.
The proposal is three tiers: Bronze, Silver and Gold. Bronze at up to five deals a year, Silver at fifteen, Gold at thirty, with better terms at each level.
Here are my opinions. We have three active partners. Three tiers for three partners means every partner is in their own tier, which is just three contracts with extra steps.
From marketing's side, tiers would need badges, a page explaining them, and an argument every time someone's one deal short of the next level.
What actually matters is whether a partner refers or resells. Tillerman refers, Northgable wants to resell. Those need different contracts, regardless of volume.
That's fair. The tiers were meant for a program with twenty partners, and we're not there yet.
So instead of Dagny's Bronze, Silver and Gold, we run two tracks: Referral and Reseller. Volume tiers can come back when we have enough partners to fill them.
Agreed. Referral and Reseller. Simple enough to put on one page.
Whatever the structure, the thing partners ask me for most is training. Tillerman's branch staff can't describe us in one sentence yet.
I'd like to record a short video for branch staff, ten minutes, on who Quillmark is for and when to mention us. They can watch it on their own time.
Tillerman would love that. Their branch managers have asked twice for something they can show new staff.
Keep it to ten minutes and keep it about the contractor's problem, not our features. Branch staff won't sit through a demo.
Ten minutes, the contractor's problem, and one slide on how to register a deal. I'll have a script for Dagny to review by the end of the month.
Which brings us to the first actual reseller. Northgable. What exactly are they asking for, and what do they offer in return?
Northgable want to buy at a discount and set their own price to the customer. They asked for thirty percent off list.
Thirty is a lot, it's more than our own sales team costs us per deal. What do they do for it?
They do the sales cycle, the setup and the data import, and they'd handle first-line support for their customers. We'd only see the escalations.
First-line support is worth something real. Some of their fleets are the kind that call us every day in the first month.
My counter would be twenty five percent. It's below their ask, and it recognises the support work.
I'd go to twenty, with a minimum of five deals a year. If they're reselling us, I want to see them actually selling us, not just holding a discount.
Five a year is reasonable. They did four in their first six months, and they've got a couple more in contracting right now.
And if they miss the minimum, they drop back to the referral track for the next year. No penalty beyond that.

Okay. Northgable gets a twenty percent reseller margin, with a minimum of five deals a year, not the thirty they asked for. They handle first-line support, and if they miss the minimum they move to the referral track.
They won't love it, but they'll sign. The margin plus the support handoff is a fair package.
On the support handoff, we need to be precise. Which tickets do Northgable's customers send to Northgable, and which come straight to us?
Everything goes to Northgable first. They escalate to us when it's a bug, a problem on our side, or a billing question about Quillmark itself.
And they get access to our escalation queue, so their tickets don't sit in the general inbox behind everything else.
I'd like a named person on their side for escalations. When something's on fire, I don't want to be emailing a shared alias.
I'll put that in the contract. A named escalation contact on their side, and a backup for holidays.
Who updates the contract? Elena, you drafted their first one, didn't you?
I did. I can turn around a revised version with the new margin and the minimum by Monday the nineteenth, if that helps.
I'd rather partner paper lived with Dagny from now on. Elena's team is busy enough with direct deals, and partners should have one person on our side.
No argument from me. I'll send Dagny the draft and my notes from their first round of comments.
Then it's mine. I'll send Northgable the revised reseller contract by Thursday the twenty-second of October, with the margin, the minimum and the support terms.
Good. The Guild next. Ilse, they asked you for something, didn't they?
They did. The Lantern Trades Guild wants a member discount on Quillmark. Something they can put in their newsletter as a membership perk.
I don't want association discounts. Once we give one association a discount, every association in every trade asks for one, and our list price stops meaning anything.
The Guild is a good partner, though. Their newsletter goes to most of the heating engineers in the region.
What if the perk isn't money? A free onboarding workshop for members, run by us, and a speaking slot at their spring conference.
Members who've been through a workshop close much faster. It's basically a pre-sales session they've asked us to run.
Then no member discount for the Guild. Instead, members get a free onboarding workshop, run by Ilse's team, and we ask for a talk at their spring conference.
I'll pitch it to them next week. I think they'll take it, they mostly wanted something to put in the newsletter.
Their spring conference is in March, and a talk there is worth more to us than a line in a newsletter. Most of the audience runs a small shop.
Then make the talk useful, not a sales pitch. If it sounds like an advert, the Guild won't invite us back next year.
Last item, and the one with money attached. Co-marketing for Q4. Ilse, what have partners asked for?
I've got three requests, and I'm asking for eighteen thousand dollars in total for Q4.
Tillerman wants to have us at their branch open days. They're opening new branches this autumn, and every opening has an open day for local contractors.
Northgable wants to run a series of customer breakfasts with fleet managers. And the Guild wants us to sponsor their regional newsletter for a quarter.
Eighteen thousand is more than our entire partner revenue covers this quarter, once the referral fees are paid. I'd cap it well below that.
The Tillerman open days are the best value on the list. Every person in the room is a contractor who already buys from Tillerman.
Then fund those properly and trim the rest. Newsletter sponsorships we can do later, if the workshops go well.
If the Guild gets the workshop instead, I can drop their newsletter request. They'd see that as the bigger offer anyway.
Then I'd say ten thousand for Q4 in total. Most of it to Tillerman, and the rest to Northgable's breakfasts.
Ten is tight, but it works without the newsletter. Six for Tillerman covers four open days with a stand and some printed material.

So the Q4 co-marketing fund is ten thousand dollars, not the eighteen thousand Ilse asked for. Six thousand of it goes to Tillerman's branch open days, and the other four thousand to the Northgable breakfasts.
Got it. I'll send each partner a short note with what we're funding and how they report back on it. Nothing fancy, one page each.
And a simple report at the end of the quarter, please. Leads from each event, and which ones turned into deals.
That's easy to track if Elena's registration form is live by then. Every lead from an event gets registered as a partner deal.
It'll be live by the thirtieth. I'll add a field for the event, so we can see which open day each deal came from.
Good. Anything else before we recap? Dagny, anything partners are asking for that we haven't covered?
A partner portal comes up every so often. A place to register deals, download slides and see their fees. But that's a next year question.
Next year, and only if we have more than three partners. For now, a shared folder and Elena's form are plenty.
Agreed. I'll keep a list of what they ask for, so we have real requirements when the time comes.
And the shared folder needs tidying before we point anyone at it. Right now it has three versions of the same slide deck, and two of them still have the old logo.
One last thing from me. Can the partners see our list prices for the new tiers before they're public? Northgable will need them to price their own offers.
Under NDA, and only after Northgable signs the revised contract. Not before.
That works. I'll share the price sheet with them the day they sign, not earlier.
Okay. Let me recap so the notes are right.
Q3 was nineteen partner deals and a hundred and sixty eight thousand dollars, with Tillerman at eleven. Referral fee goes to twelve percent, paid after the first invoice, from the first of January.

Two tracks, Referral and Reseller. Northgable at twenty percent with five deals a year, contract from Dagny by the twenty-second. No Guild discount, a workshop instead. Ten thousand for Q4 co-marketing, six of it for Tillerman.
That's everything. I'll send the partner update this week, once Tillerman's heard about the fee from me directly.
Thanks, Dagny. Good quarter, even with the corrected numbers. Tillerman especially, so let's make sure they know we noticed.
Thanks, everyone. We'll do the Q4 review in January, with the new fee and the registration form in place.

items.text: Q3 partner-sourced results: 19 deals and $168,000 in new annual contract value (first reported as 23 deals and $210,000; four were double counted with direct sales)
Tillerman Supply brought in 11 of the 19 partner deals in Q3
Referral fee rises from 10% to 12% of first-year contract value (not the proposed 15%), paid once the customer has paid its first invoice, for deals registered from January 1
Partner program has two tracks, Referral and Reseller, instead of Bronze, Silver and Gold tiers
Northgable reseller margin is 20% with a minimum of five deals a year (they asked for 30%); Northgable handles first-line support
Q4 co-marketing fund is $10,000 (Ilse asked for $18,000): $6,000 for Tillerman's branch open days, $4,000 for Northgable's breakfasts
No member discount for the Lantern Trades Guild; members get a free onboarding workshop instead
Send Northgable the revised reseller contract by Thursday, October 22
Build a deal registration form in the CRM by Friday, October 30
